title: Bligh's Open-Boat Voyage
text:
On April 28, 1789, near Tonga in the South Pacific, part of the crew of HMS Bounty mutinied under the master's mate Fletcher Christian. Lieutenant William Bligh, the ship's commander, had a sharp tongue and a temper that had worn on his men. The mutineers forced him and eighteen loyal men into the ship's launch, a boat about twenty-three feet long, with a little food and water, a compass and a quadrant, and set them adrift.

They landed first on the island of Tofua, where islanders attacked them and killed the quartermaster, John Norton. Bligh decided their only chance was to sail to the Dutch settlement at Kupang on Timor, more than three thousand nautical miles away.

He rationed food strictly, weighing out tiny portions of bread with a pair of coconut-shell scales and a pistol ball as the weight. He navigated largely from memory, through storms and rain, along the Great Barrier Reef and through the Torres Strait, and kept a careful log. He clashed with some of his men on the way.

After forty-seven days, on June 14, 1789, the launch reached Kupang. Every man who had left Tofua was still alive, though several later died of illness in the Dutch East Indies.
lesson: Leadership has many parts. You can fail badly at some, such as how you treat people, and still save lives through skill, discipline and refusal to give up.
people: William Bligh, Fletcher Christian, John Norton
location: From Tofua (Tonga) to Kupang, Timor (modern Indonesia)
source: William Bligh, A Narrative of the Mutiny on Board His Majesty's Ship Bounty (1790)
